### Chapter 19: Regime-Dependent Allocation {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
N  <- ncol(Re); dates <- zoo::index(R); X <- zoo::coredata(Re)
ep <- sim_episodes
stopifnot(N == 16L, !anyNA(Re), all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == dates))

first_oos <- 121L; win <- 60L
reb <- (first_oos - 1L):(nrow(Re) - 1L)      # weights set at the end of these months
oos <- reb + 1L                              # earn the returns of these

# The chapter's two portfolios, both as quadratic programs so that this fragment
# runs on its own in a few seconds. The chapter obtains the stress portfolio from
# optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(); the two agree to solver precision.
qp <- function(S, a) {
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(a, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
window_of <- function(t) X[(t - win + 1L):t, ]
W_calm   <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) qp(stats::cov(window_of(t)), colMeans(window_of(t)) * 1e2), numeric(N)))
W_stress <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) qp(stats::cov(window_of(t)), rep(1, N)), numeric(N)))
dimnames(W_calm) <- dimnames(W_stress) <- list(as.character(dates[reb]), colnames(Re))
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_calm), !anyNA(W_stress))

tb <- as.numeric(uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb)
turb_flag <- function(tb, q = 0.75, burn = 24L) {
  threshold <- vapply(seq_along(tb), function(t) {
    past <- tb[seq_len(t - 1L)]; past <- past[!is.na(past)]
    if (length(past) < burn) NA_real_ else stats::quantile(past, q, names = FALSE)
  }, numeric(1))
  tb > threshold
}
in_any <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(ep$episode, function(k) in_episode(dates, k)))

# The chapter's accounting, extended to weights that sum to less than one: the
# remainder is in the bill, which earns rf and is traded without cost.
cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(R))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(R)
run_path <- function(W) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(R)), nrow(W) == length(oos))
  Rm    <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, ]
  gross <- rowSums(W * Rm) + (1 - rowSums(W)) * rf[oos]
  held  <- rbind(0, (W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + gross))[-nrow(W), ])
  trade <- abs(W - held)
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[oos], gross = gross, turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2,
                 cost = as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate))
}
sharpe_of <- function(r) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf[oos])^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
switch_W <- function(s, stress = W_stress) { W <- W_calm; W[s, ] <- stress[s, ]; W }
sr_static <- sharpe_of(run_path(W_calm)$gross)
```

#### Exercise 1

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-1
thresholds <- lapply(c(0.50, 0.75, 0.90), function(q) {
  s <- turb_flag(tb, q)[reb]
  tibble::tibble(percentile = q, in_stress = mean(s),
                 sharpe   = sharpe_of(run_path(switch_W(s))$gross),
                 same_mix = sharpe_of(run_path(mean(s) * W_stress + (1 - mean(s)) * W_calm)$gross))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(timing = sharpe - same_mix)
thresholds
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-1-facts
#| include: false
th <- function(q, col) thresholds[[col]][thresholds$percentile == q]
best <- thresholds$percentile[which.max(thresholds$timing)]
```

A lower threshold flags more months, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * th(0.5, "in_stress"))`
at the median against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * th(0.9, "in_stress"))` at the
90th percentile, and a strategy that is in the minimum-variance portfolio more
often has a higher Sharpe ratio for that reason alone, which the `same_mix`
column removes. The timing column is what remains:
`r paste(sprintf("%+.2f", thresholds$timing), collapse = ", ")` at the 50th,
75th and 90th percentiles. The largest is at the
`r sprintf("%.0fth", 100 * best)` percentile, and none of the three is large
beside the standard error of a Sharpe ratio over `r length(oos)` months, about
`r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt((1 + (sr_static / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / length(oos)) * sqrt(12))`.
The threshold trades false alarms against missed months, and on this path
neither end of that trade times the market; choosing the percentile by this
table would be the parameter tuning that
@sec-25-backtesting-application warns against.

#### Exercise 2

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-2
delay <- list(`label of the month ahead (infeasible)` = in_any[oos],
              `label of the rebalancing month`        = in_any[reb])
delayed <- lapply(names(delay), function(nm) {
  p <- run_path(switch_W(delay[[nm]]))
  tibble::tibble(rule = nm, sharpe = sharpe_of(p$gross), episode = ep$label,
                 ret = vapply(ep$episode, function(e) prod(1 + p$gross[in_episode(p$date, e)]) - 1,
                              numeric(1)))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
delayed |>
  dplyr::mutate(ret = round(100 * ret, 1)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = episode, values_from = ret)
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-2-facts
#| include: false
sr_d   <- unique(delayed[, c("rule", "sharpe")])$sharpe
lost   <- (sr_d[1] - sr_d[2]) / (sr_d[1] - sr_static)
gap    <- delayed$ret[delayed$rule == names(delay)[1]] - delayed$ret[delayed$rule == names(delay)[2]]
worst  <- ep$label[which.max(gap)]
stopifnot(sr_d[1] > sr_d[2], sr_d[2] > sr_static)
```

Read at the rebalancing date, as `regime.portfolios()` reads it, the dated
label enters each episode one month late and leaves it one month late. The
Sharpe ratio falls from `r sprintf("%.3f", sr_d[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", sr_d[2])`, which is
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * lost)` of the advantage over the static policy's
`r sprintf("%.3f", sr_static)`. The loss is largest in the `r worst`, at
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(gap))` percentage points: the first month of a
short episode is a large part of it. Even a perfect dating rule that is one
month slow is still ahead of the static policy, so the delay alone does not
explain why the detected strategies of the chapter keep so little; their
false alarms, and the further month a detector needs, do.

#### Exercise 3

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-3
set.seed(1602)
n <- 1e5; stay <- c(0.98, 0.93); sigma <- c(0.06, 0.14) / sqrt(12)
u <- stats::runif(n); s <- integer(n); s[1] <- 1L
for (t in 2:n) s[t] <- if (u[t] < stay[s[t - 1L]]) s[t - 1L] else 3L - s[t - 1L]
r <- stats::rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma[s])

pi_bar <- (1 - rev(stay)) / sum(1 - stay)                      # long-run shares
formula_kurtosis <- 3 * (sum(pi_bar * sigma^4) / sum(pi_bar * sigma^2)^2 - 1)
sim <- c(share_state_2    = mean(s == 2L), formula_share = pi_bar[2],
         sample_kurtosis  = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::kurtosis(r, method = "excess")),
         formula_kurtosis = formula_kurtosis,
         acf1_returns     = stats::acf(r, 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
         acf1_squared     = stats::acf(r^2, 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
round(sim, 3)
```

The chain spends `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sim[["share_state_2"]])` of its
months in the high-volatility state, as its transition probabilities imply,
and the sample excess kurtosis of `r sprintf("%.2f", sim[["sample_kurtosis"]])`
matches the `r sprintf("%.2f", sim[["formula_kurtosis"]])` of
@eq-19-kurtosis: every draw is Gaussian and the mixture is not. The formula
would give the same number if the states were drawn independently each month.
What the persistence adds is in the last two entries. The returns themselves
are uncorrelated, at `r sprintf("%.3f", sim[["acf1_returns"]])`, and their
squares are not, at `r sprintf("%.2f", sim[["acf1_squared"]])`: large moves
follow large moves. That is volatility clustering, the reason the tails of
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application arrive as episodes rather than as
isolated months, and it is also the only reason a filter can work at all,
since a state that did not persist could be recognized but not used.

#### Exercise 4

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-4
stress_rule <- list(`minimum variance` = W_stress, `half of it, half in the bill` = 0.5 * W_stress)
derisk <- lapply(names(stress_rule), function(nm) {
  p <- run_path(switch_W(in_any[oos], stress_rule[[nm]]))
  tibble::tibble(stress = nm, sharpe = sharpe_of(p$gross),
                 drawdown = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(xts::xts(p$gross, order.by = p$date))),
                 episode = ep$label,
                 ret = vapply(ep$episode, function(e) prod(1 + p$gross[in_episode(p$date, e)]) - 1,
                              numeric(1)))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
derisk |>
  dplyr::mutate(ret = round(100 * ret, 1), drawdown = round(100 * drawdown, 1)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = episode, values_from = ret)
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-19-4-facts
#| include: false
dr <- function(nm, e) derisk$ret[derisk$stress == nm & derisk$episode == e]
ds <- function(nm, col) unique(derisk[derisk$stress == nm, c("sharpe", "drawdown")])[[col]]
stopifnot(dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "rates shock") > dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "rates shock"),
          dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "equity bear market") < dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "equity bear market"),
          dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "credit crisis") > dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "credit crisis"))
```

In the excess-return formulation of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory a weight vector that sums to one
half holds the other half in the bill, so the new stress portfolio is half the
minimum-variance weights and the accounting adds the bill's return on the
remainder. It does what moving to bonds could not: the loss inside the rates
shock falls from `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "rates shock"))`
to `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "rates shock"))`,
because the only asset that does not fall when yields rise is the one with no
duration. The price is paid in the equity bear market, where bonds rallied:
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "equity bear market"))`
against `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "equity bear market"))`.
In the credit crisis the half-invested portfolio loses less,
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[2], "credit crisis"))` against
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * dr(names(stress_rule)[1], "credit crisis"))`, because
even the minimum-variance portfolio holds some of what was falling. Over
the whole period the Sharpe ratio moves from
`r sprintf("%.3f", ds(names(stress_rule)[1], "sharpe"))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", ds(names(stress_rule)[2], "sharpe"))` and the maximum
drawdown from `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ds(names(stress_rule)[1], "drawdown"))`
to `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ds(names(stress_rule)[2], "drawdown"))`. Which
stress portfolio is right depends on which stress arrives, and a two-state
model does not say. In `PortfolioAnalytics` the specification is
`add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0.5, max_sum = 0.5)` in place
of `full_investment`, and `regime.portfolios()` accepts it beside a fully
invested calm specification, as the callout in the chapter measured.
